query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory alloys designed for fusion plasma‐facing components, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by the activation of edge dislocation slip, which is enhanced by the formation of nanoscale chemically ordered regions (e.g., B2‐like phases). These ordered regions lower local migration barriers for dislocation climb and promote more homogeneous strain distribution at high temperatures, thereby improving toughness without unduly compromising strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy or medium-entropy alloy in a predominantly disordered (single-phase BCC or FCC) state produced by rapid solidification (e.g., as-cast or minimally processed) with limited pre-existing chemical ordering.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing (or heat treatment) protocol to induce nanoscale chemical ordering (e.g., formation of fine B2-type or other ordered precipitates) without drastically altering the overall composition, while keeping an otherwise identical baseline sample in its as-cast/disordered state.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (tensile and/or compressive) performed at high temperatures typical of plasma-facing applications (e.g., 600–900 °C) under comparable strain rates, with microstructural characterization (e.g., in-situ TEM or neutron diffraction) to monitor dislocation behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale chemically ordered regions within the predominantly disordered matrix that act as mediators of edge dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, local diffusion enables the formation of nanoscale ordered regions. These regions facilitate more effective edge dislocation glide and climb by reducing local migration barriers and distributing plastic strain more uniformly, which in turn improves toughness by delaying the onset of localized failure (e.g., crack initiation).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline disordered sample, the heat-treated sample with induced nanoscale ordering will exhibit: (a) elevated high-temperature ductility/plastic strain; (b) improved fracture toughness; and (c) evidence (via in-situ microscopy) of enhanced edge dislocation mobility and more uniform dislocation spacing.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or minimally processed state in which the alloy is primarily a single disordered phase (BCC, FCC, or dual-phase) lacking significant nanoscale chemical ordering.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory high- or medium-entropy alloys (or similar fusion plasma‐facing alloys) within a high-temperature regime (approximately 600–900 °C) where diffusion is active yet controlled so as not to trigger deleterious coarsening, and when the alloy composition and processing parameters support the formation of fine, ordered precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of chemical ordering in promoting edge dislocation mediated plasticity is supported by recent studies, the quantitative impact (e.g., percentage improvement in ductility or toughness) and the sensitivity of the effect to variations in composition or processing temperature require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Use two sets of samples with the same nominal composition. One set is subjected to a precise annealing treatment intended to induce nanoscale chemical ordering. The control set is left in its as-cast or quenched disordered state. Both sets are then subjected to identical high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests at 600–900 °C) accompanied by in-situ microscopy (e.g., TEM) to observe dislocation behavior.
measurements: High-temperature stress-strain curves with focus on yield strength, work hardening rate, and ductility.
Fracture toughness and crack initiation/cycle data from mechanical tests.
Microstructural characterization (TEM, neutron diffraction) of dislocation arrangements and the presence (or absence) of nanoscale ordered regions.
Quantitative analysis of the spacing and mobility of edge dislocations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (chemically ordered) samples do not show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature ductility and toughness, nor evidence of enhanced edge dislocation mobility compared to the disordered baseline, then the hypothesis that nanoscale chemical ordering facilitates edge-dislocation-dominated deformation (and thereby governs high temperature plastic strain and toughness) is falsified.

High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprise a novel class of scientifically and technologically interesting materials. Among these, equatomic CrMnFeCoNi with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure is noteworthy because its ductility and strength increase with decreasing temperature while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures. Here we report for the first time by single-crystal micropillar compression that its bulk room temperature critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) is ~33–43 MPa, ~10 times higher than that of pure nickel. CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation. A Novel Low-Activation VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 1) High-Entropy Alloys with Excellent Heat-Softening Resistance

Abstract: The microstructure, Vickers hardness, and compressive properties of novel low-activation VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) were studied. The alloys were fabricated by vacuum-arc melting and the characteristics of these alloys were explored. The microstructures of all the alloys exhibited a typical morphology of dendritic and eutectic structures. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys are essentially single phase, consisting of a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase, whereas the VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloy contains fine, nanoscale precipitates distributed in the BCC matrix. The lattice parameters and compositions of the identified phases were investigated. The alloys have Vickers hardness values ranging from 546 HV0.2 to 1135 HV0.2 with the x ranging from 0.1 to 1, respectively. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1341 MPa and 1742 MPa, with compressive plastic strains of 42.2% and 35.7%, respectively. Strength can be controlled by edge dislocations in refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations.
